blocks.text: Multi-agent prompting assigns several distinct roles, each with its own instructions and perspective, to collaborate on a single task, a generator that drafts, a critic that reviews, closing out this module by extending the single-model techniques covered so far into a genuinely collaborative structure.

This topic covers the common generator and critic pattern, how messages pass between agent roles, why specialized roles can outperform one generalist prompt on certain tasks, and the real coordination challenge of knowing when the collaboration should stop.
1. What Multi-Agent Prompting Means

blocks.alt: Building on iterative prompting, multi-agent prompting introduces several collaborating model roles

blocks.text: Multi-agent prompting structures a task around multiple distinct roles interacting with each other, rather than a single prompt handling everything at once, each role typically has its own specific instructions, focus, and perspective on the overall task.
2. One Model, Multiple Distinct Roles

blocks.alt: One model with one role is compared against the same model playing several distinct roles

blocks.text: These separate agents do not necessarily require different underlying models, the same model can play multiple distinct roles across separate calls, each call using a different role prompt, covered in an earlier topic, to adopt a genuinely different perspective on the same shared task.
3. A Common Pattern, Generator and Critic

blocks.alt: A generator agent produces a draft, a critic agent reviews it, and the cycle continues

blocks.text: One especially common multi-agent pattern pairs a generator role, focused purely on producing content, with a critic role, focused purely on evaluating that content against specific criteria, the generator revises based on the critic feedback, and the cycle repeats, extending the self-critique idea from an earlier topic into two genuinely separate roles rather than one model critiquing itself directly.

code.content:
generator_prompt = "You are a generator. Draft a solution to: {task}"
critic_prompt = "You are a critic. Identify flaws in this solution: {draft}"

draft = model.generate(generator_prompt)
critique = model.generate(critic_prompt.format(draft=draft))
revised_draft = model.generate(generator_prompt + f"\nAddress this critique: {critique}")

blocks.text: 4. Passing Messages Between Agents

blocks.alt: Agent A output gets passed as input to agent B, producing agent B output

blocks.text: Each agent output becomes the next agent input, this connects directly to the input handling principles covered in an earlier topic, clearly marking whose output is being passed to whom, and what that receiving agent is expected to do with it.

blocks.text: 5. Why Specialized Roles Can Outperform One Generalist Prompt

blocks.alt: One generalist prompt is compared against several specialized agent roles

blocks.text: A single prompt trying to both generate and rigorously self-evaluate at once can end up doing both jobs less thoroughly than two prompts each focused on just one job, splitting generation and critique into separate, specialized roles often surfaces issues a single combined pass would miss.

blocks.title: This mirrors a familiar software engineering idea
blocks.content: Separating distinct concerns into focused, specialized components, rather than one component doing everything, tends to produce better results in prompting for largely the same reason it does in software design generally.

blocks.text: 6. The Real Cost, Multiplied Model Calls

blocks.alt: A single agent needs one call, multi-agent needs several calls with multiplied cost

blocks.text: Multi-agent prompting directly multiplies cost and latency by the number of agent calls involved, a generator and critic loop running several rounds costs meaningfully more than a single prompt, this cost has to be weighed against the quality improvement, exactly the same tradeoff covered for self-consistency and tree of thoughts earlier in this module.
7. Coordinating Agents, Knowing When to Stop

blocks.alt: No clear stopping rule risks an endless back and forth, a clear stopping rule produces clean convergence

blocks.text: Without an explicit stopping condition, a generator and critic pair could in principle continue exchanging feedback indefinitely, a clear rule, stop once the critic finds no more significant issues, or after a fixed number of rounds, is necessary to bring the collaboration to a clean, practical conclusion.
8. Multi-Agent Prompting vs the Single-Agent Techniques in This Module

Chain of thought, self-consistency, tree of thoughts, and the other techniques covered earlier in this module all operate within a single model perspective, multi-agent prompting explicitly introduces multiple distinct perspectives interacting with each other, a structural step beyond anything a single reasoning process alone can provide.
9. This Module Is Now Complete

This closes out the Advanced Prompting Techniques module, covering chain of thought, self-consistency, tree of thoughts, ReAct, plan and solve, step-by-step, least-to-most, skeleton of thoughts, reflection, self-critique, iterative, and now multi-agent prompting, the next module, Structured Outputs, shifts focus to reliably getting a model output into a specific parseable format, and the later Agent Prompting module builds much further on the multi-agent and ReAct ideas introduced here.
Worked Example

A developer building a content review tool initially uses a single prompt asking a model to both write and evaluate a piece of marketing copy, the result is serviceable but the self-evaluation feels shallow, since the same generation pass is also trying to critique itself.

Splitting this into a generator agent that focuses purely on writing the copy and a separate critic agent that focuses purely on evaluating it against brand guidelines, running for two rounds before stopping, produces noticeably more thorough critique and a stronger final revision than the single combined prompt did.
Common Mistakes

items: Running a multi-agent loop with no clear stopping condition, risking an endless, costly back and forth
Using multi-agent prompting for a simple task where one well written prompt would perform just as well at lower cost
Not giving each agent role clearly distinct, focused instructions, causing them to behave too similarly to be useful
Ignoring the multiplied cost and latency multi-agent prompting introduces compared to a single call

blocks.text: Practice

Take a task you have prompted with a single combined generate-and-check prompt, split it into a separate generator role and critic role, run one round of the exchange, and compare whether the critique feels more thorough than the original single-prompt self-evaluation.
Key Takeaway

Multi-agent prompting assigns distinct, focused roles, most commonly a generator and a critic, that collaborate across separate calls on a single task, often surfacing issues a single combined prompt would miss, at the real cost of multiplied model calls and the need for a clear rule governing when the collaboration should stop.
